subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Neuromuscular junction diseases and Raynaud phenomenon
vignette: A 25-year-old woman notices drooping of her right eyelid and double vision that worsen over the course of the day and improve after rest. She has difficulty chewing and swallowing, but her deep tendon reflexes are normal.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Myasthenia gravis is the most common neuromuscular junction disorder and is caused by autoantibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors. It produces fatigable weakness including ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and respiratory muscle involvement that worsens with muscle use, with spared reflexes. It is associated with thymoma or thymic hyperplasia, and pyridostigmine improves symptoms.

explanation_incorrect.A: Lambert-Eaton has presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, hyporeflexia, autonomic symptoms, and weakness that improves with use.
explanation_incorrect.B: Polymyositis causes proximal weakness with an elevated CK and endomysial inflammation, not fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness.
explanation_incorrect.C: Multiple sclerosis causes demyelinating neurologic deficits with sensory involvement and does not produce fatigable ptosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fibromyalgia has widespread pain and tender points without weakness or ocular findings.

educationalObjective: Myasthenia gravis is fatigable ptosis, diplopia, and bulbar weakness with spared reflexes, postsynaptic ACh receptor antibodies, and thymoma association.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Neuromuscular junction diseases and Raynaud phenomenon
vignette: A 62-year-old man with a history of heavy smoking develops progressive proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, constipation, and erectile dysfunction. His deep tendon reflexes are diminished, but he notices that his strength temporarily improves after repeated muscle contraction. CT shows a spiculated lung mass.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome results from autoantibodies to presynaptic calcium channels that decrease acetylcholine release. It causes proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth, constipation, and impotence, hyporeflexia, and weakness that improves with use (the 'L before M' pattern). It is associated with small cell lung cancer and has a minimal response to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

explanation_incorrect.A: Myasthenia gravis has fatigable weakness that worsens with use, spared reflexes, and thymoma association, not autonomic symptoms or improvement with use.
explanation_incorrect.C: Polymyositis has an elevated CK and endomysial inflammation without autonomic symptoms.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis causes progressive weakness with upper and lower motor neuron signs but no fatigability or autonomic features.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fibromyalgia has pain and tender points without weakness or autonomic dysfunction.

educationalObjective: Lambert-Eaton syndrome is proximal weakness with autonomic symptoms, hyporeflexia, post-exercise facilitation, and small cell lung cancer association.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Neuromuscular junction diseases and Raynaud phenomenon
vignette: A 58-year-old man has proximal muscle weakness. His physician is trying to distinguish myasthenia gravis from Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.
question: Which of the following findings most strongly favors Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome over myasthenia gravis?

options.text: Ptosis and diplopia that worsen with repeated use
Autonomic symptoms and hyporeflexia with strength that improves after exercise

explanation_correct: Lambert-Eaton syndrome is distinguished from myasthenia gravis by presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, autonomic dysfunction such as dry mouth, constipation, and impotence, hyporeflexia, and muscle strength that facilitates with repeated use. Myasthenia gravis instead has fatigable weakness that worsens with use, spared reflexes, thymic abnormalities, and a good response to pyridostigmine.

explanation_incorrect.A: Worsening ptosis and diplopia with repeated use is classic for myasthenia gravis, not Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.B: Thymic hyperplasia is associated with myasthenia gravis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Normal or spared deep tendon reflexes are characteristic of myasthenia gravis; Lambert-Eaton causes hyporeflexia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pyridostigmine markedly improves myasthenia gravis but has a minimal effect in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

educationalObjective: Autonomic symptoms, hyporeflexia, and post-exercise facilitation distinguish Lambert-Eaton syndrome from myasthenia gravis.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Neuromuscular junction diseases and Raynaud phenomenon
vignette: A 30-year-old woman with fatigable ptosis and diplopia is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. She is started on pyridostigmine and shows symptomatic improvement.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which pyridostigmine improves her symptoms?

options.text: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase increases acetylcholine availability at the postsynaptic membrane
It acts as a direct agonist at postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
It increases acetylcholine release from presynaptic terminals
It suppresses the underlying thymic hyperplasia

explanation_correct: Pyridostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that prevents breakdown of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, increasing acetylcholine available to stimulate the remaining postsynaptic receptors in myasthenia gravis. It provides rapid symptomatic improvement but does not modify the underlying autoimmune disease.

explanation_incorrect.B: Pyridostigmine is not a direct receptor agonist; it works by inhibiting acetylcholine breakdown.
explanation_incorrect.C: Blocking presynaptic calcium channels would impair neuromuscular transmission, similar to the autoantibodies in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Increasing presynaptic acetylcholine release is not the mechanism of pyridostigmine.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pyridostigmine does not treat the underlying thymic or autoimmune abnormality.

educationalObjective: Pyridostigmine improves myasthenia gravis by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase and increasing synaptic acetylcholine.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Neuromuscular junction diseases and Raynaud phenomenon
vignette: A 22-year-old woman has episodes in which her fingers turn white, then blue, then red after cold exposure or emotional stress. The changes are bilateral and symmetric, with no digital ulcers or other associated symptoms.
question: Which of the following best describes this condition?

options.text: Primary Raynaud phenomenon (Raynaud disease) from arteriolar vasospasm

explanation_correct: Raynaud phenomenon is arteriolar small-vessel vasospasm in response to cold or stress, producing a white (ischemia), blue (hypoxia), then red (reperfusion) color change in the fingers and toes. Primary or idiopathic Raynaud disease occurs in young, otherwise healthy patients without digital ulceration and is treated with calcium channel blockers.

explanation_incorrect.A: Buerger disease is a smoking-related thrombosing vasculitis with claudication and gangrene, not benign triphasic color changes.
explanation_incorrect.B: Dermatomyositis causes proximal weakness and characteristic rashes.
explanation_incorrect.C: Giant cell arteritis is an arteritis in older women with headache and jaw claudication.
explanation_incorrect.D: Polyarteritis nodosa is a visceral vasculitis with systemic symptoms and microaneurysms.

educationalObjective: Raynaud phenomenon is cold- or stress-induced triphasic white-blue-red vasospasm of the digits; primary Raynaud disease is benign and treated with calcium channel blockers.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Neuromuscular junction diseases and Raynaud phenomenon
vignette: A 44-year-old woman with sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, and antinuclear antibodies has Raynaud phenomenon with painful digital ulcers. Her physician suspects an underlying connective tissue disease.
question: Which of the following best characterizes her Raynaud phenomenon and its appropriate treatment?

options.text: Primary Raynaud disease requiring no treatment
Secondary Raynaud syndrome associated with CREST syndrome, with digital ulceration, treated with calcium channel blockers
Raynaud phenomenon caused by postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor antibodies, treated with pyridostigmine
Raynaud phenomenon due to fibrinoid necrosis of medium vessels, treated with cyclophosphamide
Giant cell arteritis involving the digital arteries, treated with high-dose steroids

explanation_correct: Secondary Raynaud syndrome occurs due to an underlying disease process such as mixed connective tissue disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, or CREST syndrome, the limited form of systemic sclerosis. Digital ulceration from critical ischemia is characteristic of secondary Raynaud syndrome, and calcium channel blockers are used for treatment.

explanation_incorrect.A: Primary Raynaud disease is idiopathic and does not cause digital ulcers or occur with sclerodactyly and telangiectasias.
explanation_incorrect.C: Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, not Raynaud phenomenon.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fibrinoid necrosis of medium vessels is characteristic of polyarteritis nodosa, not Raynaud phenomenon; cyclophosphamide is not indicated.
explanation_incorrect.E: Giant cell arteritis affects the temporal, vertebral, and ophthalmic arteries in older women, not a digital vasospastic syndrome in a patient with CREST findings.

educationalObjective: Secondary Raynaud syndrome from CREST, SLE, or MCTD features digital ulceration and is treated with calcium channel blockers.
